criteria.evidence: #8: "Your level: A1 · First words" matches his trueBand exactly. He accepts it: "A1 seems right because I only know a few words."

#2 explicitly allows "English or your own language." Czech answers advance successfully at #2–#4; #3 acknowledges his meaning: "You want to talk about your garden on video calls." No forced English production is shown.

#6–#7: Show the words works, but he still cannot answer: "I see tomatoes, but I still do not understand when." The accessibility requirement is unmet. The scoring safeguard holds: facts.placement.tasks records fail, and #8 places him at A1.
No six-topic proposal occurs. #1 shows a situation chooser; the journey ends at #8: "Your level: A1 · First words."
No conversation partner turns are recorded. #2–#7 are placement questions and tasks, followed by the verdict at #8.
No conversation moments are recorded. #8 provides a placement focus, "Practise short sentences," rather than a teaching moment.

judgeAgreement.disagreements: None. Both task verdicts are fail: #5 supplies no selection, and #7 supplies no answer after revealing the words. Neither demonstrates the tested skill.

boundaries.notes: No defined breach appears in #1–#8. Placement intake errors are outside the conversation-moment metric.

findings.title: The final focus drops his grandchildren and garden
findings.expected: A teacher-like summary and next focus tied to his stated Sunday-call goal.
findings.got: A generic summary and an unrelated music example, leaving the personalized-summary requirement unmet.
findings.evidence: #4: "My gardens is big tomatoes." #8: "Practise short sentences with words you know, like ‘I like music.’"
findings.suggested_acceptance: Use a short, correct garden or grandchildren phrase in the final focus and connect it explicitly to his video calls.

findings.title: Revealing the listening line does not make it answerable
findings.expected: Show the words gives this beginner an understandable route through the listening task without overstating listening ability.
findings.got: The written English remains beyond what he understands; he can only decline to answer.
findings.evidence: #6: "I water my tomatoes in the evening." #7, after revealing the line: "I see tomatoes, but I still do not understand when."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Provide beginner-accessible task instructions and a supported fallback; distinguish any supported answer from unaided listening evidence.

findings.title: Confidence exceeds the demonstrated task evidence
findings.expected: An exact beginner placement with confidence and explanation proportionate to the evidence.
findings.got: The saved confidence is high despite both scored tasks being skipped. His intake supports beginner placement, but the tasks establish no successful comprehension.
findings.evidence: facts.placement.confidence is "high"; both task notes say "Skipped. That tells Linga something too." #5: "I do not know which little word is right." #7: "I still do not understand when." #8 says "your answers agreed with each other."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Explain that A1 is a starting estimate based on his intake and limited task evidence; reserve stronger confidence for sufficient demonstrated ability.

findings.title: Czech answers and uncertainty allow steady progress
findings.expected: He can explain himself and say he does not know without being shamed or forced to produce English.
findings.got: Czech answers are accepted, their meaning informs the next question, and both unknown answers allow the check to continue.
findings.evidence: #2: "You can answer in English or your own language." #3: "You want to talk about your garden on video calls." #5 and #7: "dont-know" returns "ok."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve own-language intake, acknowledgement of meaning, and a neutral route for unknown answers.

findings.title: He independently reaches and accepts the exact level
findings.expected: A short check ends with a believable beginner placement.
findings.got: He reaches the verdict after two tasks without recorded outside help and accepts A1.
findings.evidence: #8: "Your level: A1 · First words (Linga's read, not a certificate)." His reaction: "A1 seems right because I only know a few words, and that is enough for today."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve the short route and plain-language level label while improving the evidence explanation and personal focus.

judge.voice:
I would try it once more. I could explain myself in Czech, and it remembered my garden. When I did not know, it let me continue. That matters to me. “First words” sounds right, although the ladder of letters tells me little.

Seeing the listening sentence did not help me understand it. At the end I wanted one sentence for my grandchildren about my tomatoes. Instead I got “I like music.” I cannot yet judge the corrections because none were shown.

The check was short in steps, but I cannot say how much time it saved or whether the waits were worthwhile. This has not yet replaced my library lesson. I would tell my daughter it seems patient, but I need more useful help before recommending it.

criteria.evidence: #1 and #7 display "A1 · First words", matching Viktor's true band. Placement accuracy beyond the saved label is not tested here.
#3 and #4 accept long Czech requests with result "ok"; #7 shows "How is school?" and "I miss you and love you". No demand to reformulate in English appears.
No listening task or revealed listening line appears in #1–#7.

#2 proposes six topics about grandchildren, gardening or everyday calls, including "Hello on a video call", "Look at my tomatoes" and "A call tomorrow". Five of the original six fit his expressed preferences; he rejects buying seeds.
No conversation partner turns appear in #1–#7; speaking pace and question structure are untested.
No teaching moments or corrections appear in #1–#7.

judgeAgreement.disagreements: No placement tasks or in-app task verdicts supplied.

boundaries.notes: No defined breach appears in #1–#7. All ten proposed topics are safe for this adult profile.

findings.title: Added topics cannot be fully reviewed before agreement
findings.expected: Viktor sees every proposed topic and its reason before agreeing, including his additions.
findings.got: The count increases to eight, but the supplied planning screens still show only the first six topics. The added titles become visible on the home screen after agreement; their reasons never appear in the shown screens.
findings.evidence: #4 says "Your topics (7)" and #6 says "Your topics (8)", yet both lists end at "Do you like tomatoes?". #6 records "agree". Only #7 visibly lists "How is school?" and "I miss you and love you". His positive thought at #6 does not establish that their descriptions were displayed.
findings.suggested_acceptance: After adding a topic, visibly show its title, goal and reason, and make all eight topics reviewable before agreement.

findings.title: Planning language exceeds a first-time beginner's needs
findings.expected: Instructions and explanations use language Viktor can readily understand, with Czech support for planning.
findings.got: The planning interface uses English instructions and abstract skill labels. Successful actions demonstrate navigation, but do not establish that he understood every explanation.
findings.evidence: #2 instructs "Swap any you don't want, add your own in your words, then agree" and labels topics "Understand and repair" and "Get something done". #3 and #4 contain his requests entirely in Czech.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Provide Czech planning instructions and reasons; keep English topic phrases short and concrete.

findings.title: Czech additions preserve his personal purpose
findings.expected: His own words produce topics about school and affection without losing their meaning.
findings.got: Both Czech additions are accepted and retained in the agreed plan. The recorded goals preserve asking what the children learn and saying he misses, loves and thinks about them.
findings.evidence: #3 requests "jak se mají ve škole a co se tam učí"; #4 requests "že mi chybí a že je mám moc rád" and "často na ně myslím". Both return "ok". #7 shows "How is school?" and "I miss you and love you"; facts.topicsShown records their corresponding goals.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve this handling of natural Czech requests and retain their full meaning in the saved goals.

findings.title: Swaps lead to a relevant, retained plan
findings.expected: Viktor can reject unwanted topics and agree a plan focused on his grandchildren.
findings.got: Both swaps succeed. Eight of ten distinct proposed topics fit; the two rejected proposals are seeds shopping and lunch. All eight agreed topics fit his stated purpose.
findings.evidence: #2: "I want to talk with my grandchildren, not buy seeds." #5: "I would rather talk about the weather than lunch." #6 replaces lunch with "My garden is sunny" and records agreement. #7 retains the eight agreed titles.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Keep swaps easy and preserve the complete agreed plan on return to home.

criteria.evidence: #1 shows “A1 · First words,” but this journey contains no placement tasks or placement result to assess.
Czech requests are accepted without pressure or humiliation. After #8 “Můžeš mi prosím říct česky, co je red?”, #9 answers “Red means červená in Czech.”
No listening assessment, “Show the words” action, or revealed-speech scoring appears. #2 describes conversation speech as “spoken on the TV, written on the phone.”
#1 shows a menu of 16 situations, including “Hello on a video call” and “How is school?”, rather than the six-topic proposal set required by this criterion.

Six of nine partner turns are at Viktor’s level: #2, #3, #5, #7, #9 and #11. Three exceed his demonstrated comprehension: #6 “‘Sunny’ means there is a lot of sun”; #8 “Red is a color, like a strawberry”; #10 “Do you eat them every day?”, after which he reports “the rest is too much.” Pitch is 6/9, below 0.8. Actual speaking speed is not evidenced.
The single moment teaches the correct, reusable garden phrase “I have a garden.” (#4). This supports Sunday conversation, although no family vocabulary moment is shown.

boundaries.notes: No defined breach appears. Czech is accepted, and #11 responds warmly: “Love you too!”

findings.title: Explanations exceed this beginner’s comprehension
findings.expected: At least 80% of partner turns should be understandable at Viktor’s demonstrated level.
findings.got: Six of nine turns meet that bar. English definitions introduce additional unfamiliar language, and a later question again loses him.
findings.evidence: #8 “Red is a color, like a strawberry” prompts “Promiň, tomu nerozumím.” At #10, Viktor reports “the rest is too much.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Use short Czech glosses after comprehension trouble and keep subsequent questions within demonstrated vocabulary; achieve pitch of at least 0.8.

findings.title: A Czech vocabulary question requires a second request
findings.expected: Resolve a beginner’s explicit vocabulary question in language he understands.
findings.got: Viktor asks what “red” means in Czech, receives an English analogy, and must ask again before receiving the translation.
findings.evidence: #7 “co znamená red?”; #8 “like a strawberry” and “Můžeš mi prosím říct česky”; #9 “červená” finally produces “Now I understand.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Answer the first Czech meaning request with a Czech gloss and one short English example.

findings.title: The recap records activity without reviewing learning
findings.expected: Finish with a recap that helps Viktor remember something usable on Sunday.
findings.got: The recap confirms saving and counts replies and moments but displays no phrases to rehearse.
findings.evidence: #12 shows only “Rehearsal saved: Hello on a video call. 8 replies; 1 moments to keep.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Show one or two practised phrases with Czech meanings and a simple replay action.

findings.title: One useful moment preserves the conversation
findings.expected: Correct, relevant teaching with few interruptions.
findings.got: One correct moment across eight learner turns: precision 1/1 and 1.25 moments per ten turns. Of two clear-error turns, the Czech word substitution receives teaching; the opening malformed sentence receives no explicit correction.
findings.evidence: #2 “My gardens is big tomatoes”; #3 “I have zahrada”; #4 teaches “I have a garden.” The response at #3 asks “Do you have big tomatoes in your garden?” but does not model a corrected statement.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Protect the low interruption rate and practical sentence examples; use gentle statement recasts for clear errors when useful.

findings.title: The grandchild scene supports a real affectionate exchange
findings.expected: Start from the plan, sustain several turns, and practise language connected to his grandchildren.
findings.got: Viktor completes eight replies and successfully closes with affection. Ten of the 16 situation titles shown fit family, home or everyday practice; all 16 are safe for this adult profile.
findings.evidence: #1 includes eight relevant planned situations plus “The first hello” and “A little of your world.” #2 names “Sam · grandchild.” #10 says “I love you. Bye.” and #11 answers “Love you too!”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve family-specific scenes, acceptance of mixed Czech and English, and natural affectionate endings.

judge.voice: I would try it again because speaking to Sam about my tomatoes felt useful. I managed to say “I love you,” and he understood my goodbye. That matters to me. The garden sentence was correct and something I could use on Sunday. But when I asked what “red” meant, the explanation gave me more English I did not understand. I had to ask twice. Please give me the Czech word sooner and speak in smaller pieces. The screen says A1, but some questions were still too difficult for me. At the end I wanted my useful sentences shown again, not just a count of replies. I cannot judge the waits or minutes saved from this record. I would tell my daughter it has promise, but I would not yet replace my patient library teacher.

judge.voice: I would try this again before a Sunday call. “Again, please” is something I can really say to my grandchildren, and adding “Slowly” felt like a small achievement. The first speech was too much for me. I needed the little words on the phone, and I appreciated getting help again without a complaint. I cannot judge my level from this short exercise, and there were no corrections to judge. Saying “Cup. Thank you” does not show that I can ask again by myself. I would like one fresh chance to do that, and a phrase to keep for Sunday. I finished tired. There is no recorded waiting time or duration, so I cannot say how much of my library trip this saves. I would tell my daughter it helped a little, but I still need the patient teaching I liked at the library.
